claim.statement: The v39 verification pass strengthens the official-enforcement side of the Starlink crackdown but not the legal-proof side: ILNA/Police reported 46 networked Starlink sellers arrested across 19 provinces with 139 devices/routers seized, ILNA/Intelligence Ministry said hundreds of enemy-sent Starlink systems had been identified and would continue to be tracked, Tehran police-linked reports describe the Fereshteh arrest, three northwest-Tehran guild units sealed, and a Yusefabad apartment framed as a spy base, and Bartarinha/Fars reported 6 Yazd suspects, 6 devices, 61 blocked bank accounts, and prosecutor referral; however v39 searches did not surface public court records, indictments, named defense counsel, family statements, or independent evidence verifying the espionage facts behind those police claims.
claim.subject: Iran Starlink enforcement public record
claim.object: police and intelligence statements rather than independent legal corroboration

evidence.summary: The notes record Exa searches for court, prosecutor, indictment, lawyer, family, and account-freeze terms and the absence of public legal corroboration in the result set.
ILNA/Police quoted Radan saying 46 Starlink seller-network actors in 19 provinces were arrested and 139 Starlink devices/routers were seized.
ILNA carried a Ministry of Intelligence statement saying hundreds of enemy-sent Starlink systems were identified/seized and tracking would continue.
Bartarinha/Fars reported Yazd police claims of 6 devices, 6 suspects, 61 blocked bank accounts, and referral to the provincial prosecutor.

information_depth.rationale: The claim is about the source ecology and official enforcement reports, not about proving the espionage allegations.

assessment.uncertainty: Underlying espionage facts remain unverified until court files, defense access, named family/lawyer statements, or independent technical evidence appear.

claim.statement: Persian legal/police reporting describes a broad Starlink penalty ladder under the 1404 intensified espionage/cooperation law: Tabnak/Mehr's lawyer explainer says personal use, carrying, holding, buying, selling, or importing unauthorized satellite-internet tools can bring degree-6 imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years plus seizure, distribution/installation/import-for-distribution can bring degree-5 imprisonment of 2 to 5 years, and intent to confront the system or espionage can trigger severe punishment including execution or degree-4 imprisonment of 5 to 10 years; the Yazd police account adds that wartime/security conditions can intensify punishment by up to three degrees.
claim.subject: Iran Starlink criminal exposure
claim.object: personal-use imprisonment to espionage-linked death-penalty exposure

evidence.summary: Tabnak/Mehr quoted a lawyer describing Article 5 categories and penalties for personal use, distribution, and espionage/anti-system intent.
The Yazd police report restated Starlink criminalization and said wartime/security conditions can intensify punishment by up to three degrees.

information_depth.rationale: The row uses a media legal explainer and police-reported legal framing; it should be checked against the statutory text.

assessment.uncertainty: Exact statutory language and judicial practice still need direct legal-text and case-record confirmation.

claim.statement: The Hossam Aladdin Starlink-related death report is now a high-visibility but contested allegation: on 1 May, IranWire reported that a 40-year-old father linked to the Aladdin mall family died after security forces beat him during a Starlink-related home search, while Iran International reported a received-message account saying he was violently arrested after trying to recover seized electronics and was beaten to death at home during a search; xPool v39 emitted 160 items and found 68 Hossam/Aladdin-coded posts amplifying the claim, but also 12 skepticism or alternative-motive posts, and v39 did not find official confirmation, named family/lawyer confirmation, court records, or a clean forensic/burial record; IranWire's article also contains an impossible burial-date line, 'Wednesday 9 Esfand 1405,' inside an 11 Ordibehesht 1405 article.
claim.subject: Hossam Aladdin death-in-custody allegation

evidence.summary: IranWire reported Hossam Aladdin's death after a Starlink-related search/beating, but includes an impossible burial date inside the article.
Iran International reported a received-message account of violent arrest, seized electronics, home search, and death after severe beating.
The May 2 xPool sample reached 160 items and was dominated by Hossam amplification, with some skepticism and no direct legal/family record.
The notes record source-hygiene concerns and the absence of official, family, lawyer, or forensic confirmation in v39 searches.

information_depth.rationale: Two opposition/exile outlets and a large social sample carry the allegation, but the story lacks named-source, legal, forensic, family, or official confirmation and contains one date inconsistency.

assessment.uncertainty: Upgrade only with family/lawyer identity, official denial/confirmation, cemetery/burial record, coroner detail, or multiple accountable source-near confirmations.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v39 - Starlink crackdown is real, legal proof is thin
synthesis.summary: The thirty-ninth pass tests whether Starlink enforcement can be verified beyond police/state-media wording. The enforcement campaign is real as official behavior: police/intelligence statements now describe Fereshteh, northwest-Tehran commercial units, Yusefabad, Yazd account freezes, 46 seller-network arrests across 19 provinces, 139 seized devices/routers, and intelligence-ministry tracking of hundreds of systems. The law frame is also explicit: unauthorized satellite-internet tools are described as carrying penalties from personal-use imprisonment and seizure up to wartime/espionage exposure to much harsher punishment. But the public legal record is thin. v39 did not surface court records, indictments, named defense counsel, family statements, or independent technical proof behind the espionage allegations. The explosive new layer is Hossam Aladdin: IranWire and Iran International report a Starlink-related death after arrest/search/beating, and xPool shows broad amplification, but the report remains contested because there is no official/family/lawyer/forensic confirmation and IranWire contains an impossible burial-date line. Net: Starlink has become a security-law tripwire and propaganda object; what is verified is the crackdown, not yet the facts alleged inside individual espionage cases or the Hossam death narrative.
synthesis.limitations: This pass is strong on public-source topology and official enforcement claims, weak on underlying case truth. Court records, lawyers, family members, coroner/cemetery records, and technical evidence remain missing. Hossam Aladdin should be handled as a contested high-importance allegation until direct confirmation appears. Watch for official denial, family/lawyer names, burial imagery with dates, judiciary filings, and whether Starlink cases bridge into anti-execution, Internet Pro refusal, or bazaar/mobile-market discourse.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines existing KNB Starlink rows, fresh Exa/crawl evidence, a completed 160-item xPool sample, and explicit source-hygiene constraints.

operations.rationale: The claim directly answers the verification question by separating official enforcement evidence from missing court/legal corroboration.
The legal penalty ladder explains why court records and exact charges matter for Starlink cases.
The Hossam allegation is the highest-severity Starlink claim found in v39 and shows the cost of missing direct family/legal/official confirmation.
If confirmed, the Hossam death report could bridge Starlink enforcement into anti-execution and death-in-custody mobilization.
Starlink enforcement and Internet Pro management are two sides of the same tiered-access control problem.

operations.reason: v39 moves from bread/food containment to the Starlink enforcement verification question and separates verified official crackdown behavior from unverified espionage facts and contested death-in-custody reporting.
